title: Human brains construct individualized global rankings from identical few-shot learning input
experiments_summary:
The study used two main experimental approaches: a preregistered behavioral paradigm and an MEG neuroimaging study.

**Behavioral Experiment:** Two independent cohorts (total N=77 after exclusions) completed a two-phase task. In the few-shot learning phase, participants viewed eight pre-determined, non-adjacent item pairs (out of 28 possible pairs) presented across four blocks, each pair shown once per block, without requiring a response. Items were framed as movies with box office scores shown as bar comparisons. In the testing phase, participants judged all 28 possible pairwise combinations across 10 blocks without feedback. All participants received identical training pairs: (A,F), (B,C), (B,E), (C,G), (D,F), (D,G), (E,H), (A,H).

**Behavioral Analyses:** (1) Beta distribution fitting was applied to accuracy distributions for each pair across subjects to classify distributions as unimodal, high-accuracy, low-accuracy, or bimodal. (2) Error consistency was quantified by computing the proportion of consistently erroneous pairs per participant across multiple thresholds (60–100%). (3) Circular triads analysis was used to assess internal self-consistency of inferred rankings, with a self-consistency coefficient calculated and compared against a permutation-based null distribution (1,000 shuffles). (4) HodgeRank method was used to reconstruct each participant's subjective global ranking from pairwise judgments. Inter-subject ranking similarity was quantified using Kendall's tau. (5) Computational models—Q-learning, Beta-Q, Betasort, distance-averaging, and correct-ranking models—were fit to trial-by-trial choices via maximum likelihood estimation, then used to simulate behavior for comparison with human data.

**MEG Experiment:** An independent cohort (N=27 after exclusions) completed three sequential phases under continuous MEG recording using a 306-channel Elekta Neuromag system sampled at 1,000 Hz. The pre-learning phase involved a sequential comparison task based on real-world object size (5 blocks × 81 images). The learning phase replicated the behavioral paradigm exactly. The post-learning phase repeated the sequential comparison task using the newly learned artificial rankings. MEG data were preprocessed with Maxfilter, bandpass filtered (1–40 Hz), downsampled to 200 Hz, epoched (−200 to 1,500 ms), and cleaned via ICA.

**MEG Analyses:** Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) was performed at each time point. Neural RDMs were constructed from spatial patterns across 204 gradiometer sensors using 1-minus-Pearson-correlation dissimilarity. Three model RDMs were constructed: low-level visual similarity (pixel/RGB cosine dissimilarity), real-world size rank (absolute rank differences, shared across participants), and subjective rank (individual-specific, derived from each participant's reconstructed ranking). Multiple linear regression was run at each time point with these three model RDMs as predictors of each participant's neural RDM. For visual similarity and real-world size, beta coefficients were averaged across pre- and post-learning phases; for subjective ranking, post-minus-pre-learning beta differences were computed. Statistical significance was assessed via cluster-based permutation testing (100,000 sign-flips, cluster threshold p<0.05). A sensor-level searchlight RSA was conducted by constructing local neural RDMs from each sensor and its neighbors averaged over significant time windows. A cross-subject permutation test (1,000 iterations of shuffling subjective-rank model assignments across participants) validated that neural effects were specific to each individual's own ranking.
